title: Arise, Shine: The Nations Come to Zion's Light
summary: Jerusalem is told to arise and shine because the glory of the LORD has risen on her while darkness covers the earth. Nations and kings come to her light, bringing her scattered children home and carrying wealth from Arabia, the sea, and Lebanon to adorn God's house. Her former oppressors bow to her, her walls are called Salvation and her gates Praise, and in the end she needs neither sun nor moon, because the LORD himself will be her everlasting light.
story: Chapter 59 ended with the Redeemer coming to Zion. Chapter 60 describes his arrival as a sunrise. It is the first of three chapters (60 to 62) that form the bright center of the book's final part, surrounded by chapters of lament and judgment. Much of its imagery gathers earlier promises: the nations streaming to Zion (2:2-4), the wealth of the nations, the return of exiles carried on the arm (49:22), and the light that the Servant was to bring to the nations (42:6; 49:6). Here that light has come, and it shines from Jerusalem.
historical:
For the community that returned to Jerusalem after 539 BC, the city was a humble place. The rebuilt temple, finished about 516/515 BC, was plainer than Solomon's (Ezra 3:12 records older people weeping when they saw its foundation), the walls lay in ruins until Nehemiah rebuilt them around 445 BC, and Judah was a small province of the Persian Empire. A chapter promising that kings would serve Jerusalem and nations would bring their wealth would have seemed extravagant against that background, which is part of its force.

The peoples named are real and well known in the Old Testament. Midian and Ephah (verse 6) were tribes of the Arabian desert descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:2-4). Sheba, in southern Arabia, was famous for gold, spices, and incense, and its queen once visited Solomon (1 Kings 10). Kedar and Nebaioth (verse 7) were Arab tribes descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13). Tarshish (verse 9) was a distant port reached by large ships, often located in the far west of the Mediterranean, possibly in Spain, though its location is debated.
cultural:
Wealth in the ancient world moved by caravan and by ship. Camel caravans carried gold, frankincense, and spices along the Arabian trade routes, and frankincense, a fragrant resin from trees of southern Arabia, was burned in temple worship (Exodus 30:34). Timber from Lebanon, especially cedar and cypress, was the prized building material for palaces and temples; Solomon imported it for the first temple (1 Kings 5:6-10). The chapter pictures all these goods flowing toward God's house rather than toward an emperor's capital.

In a world of warfare, a city's gates were shut at night and in danger; open gates day and night (verse 11) meant complete security and constant welcome. Nations bowing at someone's feet was the standard picture of submission to a conqueror, and verse 14 reverses Jerusalem's humiliation by her former oppressors. Naming walls and gates (verse 18) followed the ancient custom of giving city gates names, as Jerusalem's gates had (Nehemiah 3).
literary: The chapter is a single sustained poem addressed to Zion as a woman (“you” is feminine singular throughout). It is framed by light: it opens with light rising on her (verses 1 to 3) and closes with the LORD as her everlasting light replacing the sun and moon (verses 19 and 20). Between these, it moves through three waves of arrival: her children and the wealth of the sea and the desert (4 to 9), foreigners and kings who rebuild and serve (10 to 14), and a series of exchanges in which everything old is replaced by something better, bronze with gold, iron with silver, violence with peace (15 to 18). The final verses return to the people themselves, the planting of the LORD.

outline.t: Arise, shine: the glory of the LORD has risen
Children and wealth come by caravan and by ship
Foreigners rebuild, kings serve, oppressors bow
Forsaken no longer: walls called Salvation, gates called Praise

doctrines.note: Nations come to Zion's light because the LORD's glory has risen on her, not because of her own brilliance. God's people are a light for the nations only as they reflect his light.
The chapter pictures a future so complete that sorrow ends and God himself replaces the sun. Biblical hope is not escape from the world but the renewal of the world with God fully present in it.
Kings and nations serve Zion and bring their wealth to God's house. The kingdom of God is pictured as a city into which the treasures of every culture are gathered and made holy.

words.note: Or, light. It appears five times in the chapter and frames it: “your light has come” (verse 1) and “the LORD will be your everlasting light” (verses 19 and 20). The light is not simply brightness but God's presence and favor, the reverse of the darkness that covers the peoples.

Kavod, glory, from a root meaning heavy. God's glory is the weight and visible splendor of his presence, as when it filled the tabernacle and Solomon's temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11). Here it rises on Zion like the sun, and the prophet Ezekiel had seen it leave the temple before the exile (Ezekiel 10).

Paar, to beautify or glorify. It appears four times: God will adorn his glorious house (verse 7), he has glorified Zion (verse 9), Lebanon's trees will come to adorn his sanctuary (verse 13), and all this is so that he himself may be glorified (verse 21). Zion's beauty exists for God's glory.

christ: When the magi come from the east to worship the infant Jesus, bringing gold and frankincense along with myrrh (Matthew 2:1-11), Matthew's readers could hardly miss the echo of verse 6, where nations bring gold and frankincense to the LORD. The chapter's vision is taken up most fully in Revelation 21 and 22: the new Jerusalem has no need of sun or moon because the glory of God gives it light and the Lamb is its lamp; its gates are never shut, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it (Revelation 21:23-26). Jesus called himself the light of the world (John 8:12) and his followers a city set on a hill (Matthew 5:14). The link with the magi is a thematic echo; the use in Revelation is deliberate and sustained.

hard.q: Is this chapter promising Jewish domination over other nations?
hard.a: Some verses, read alone, sound like a reversal of empire: nations serve Zion, kings bow, and the nation that will not serve will perish (verse 12). Readers respond differently. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters read the chapter as a promise of Israel's literal restoration and preeminence in the age to come. Many others note that the chapter's center is not Israel's power but God's glory: the nations come to the light of the LORD, bring gifts for his house, and proclaim his praises (verse 6), and the result is peace and righteousness, not violence (verses 17 and 18). On this reading the language of submission is the ancient idiom for acknowledging the true king, and those who come are worshipers, not slaves. The chapter also belongs with passages such as 2:2-4 and 56:6-7, where the nations join Israel in worship. What the chapter plainly rejects is a world where Zion is forsaken and violence rules.

questions: The command in verse 1 is to arise and shine because light has come, not to produce light. How does that change the way you think about your influence on others?
Verses 17 and 18 describe exchanges: gold for bronze, peace for violence. What exchange do you most long for God to make in your life or community?
What would it mean for your church to have gates that are never shut?
